Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (NovaPay - Platform), Elena Gomez (NovaPay - ML Eng), Samir Khan (NovaPay - Infra), Priya Reddy (NovaPay - PM)

Summary (auto): weekly POC sync focusing on latency tuning. Reviewed recent TTFT numbers, discussed enabling streaming, impact of sequence length and kernel choice, and next steps for running focused benchmarks and infra tweaks.

00:00 Sofia Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick roll call?
00:06 Ravi Patel: hey, ravi here, elena and samir on my side, priya too
00:10 Elena Gomez: hi all
00:12 Marcus Li: marcus from redwood, i'll take the deep dive bits on kernels and streaming

02:05 Sofia Chen: quick agenda, recap last week, go over the TTFT numbers you sent, talk streaming vs non-streaming, sequence length tradeoffs, kernel choices, and action items

04:30 Elena Gomez: so we ran the initial TTFTs on our dev cluster, numbers are roughly 220ms cold, warm to first token around 85ms on average for a single long prompt (~1k tokens), but our front-end cares about conversational 1-token TTFT when the user types a message
04:50 Samir Khan: yeah and i think our p99 is spiking to like 600-700ms sometimes when we get bursts, not sure if thats warm vs batching behavior or kv cache warmup

06:15 Marcus Li: ok that tracks. couple of clarifications: when you say 1-token TTFT did you run with streaming enabled or just request the whole answer? streaming makes a big difference in perceived TTFT because we can flush the first token as soon as it's available
06:34 Elena Gomez: this was with full response mode, not streaming. we didn't enable streaming yet cause we were worried about proxying and chunk boundaries in our frontend

08:00 Marcus Li: cool. if you switch to streaming we typically see first-byte/first-token times drop by 30-60% depending on model and kernel. one caveat is models compiled with fused attention kernels sometimes have higher single-token latency but better throughput at scale
08:22 Ravi Patel: fused kernels? can you explain real quick like tradeoffs?
08:30 Marcus Li: sure; fused kernels fuse multiple ops for a single step which reduces per-token compute but can increase startup cost; unfused or generic kernels might be faster for very short sequences or where prefetching and small-batch execution is important. quantization also interacts here — int8 can be slightly faster but sometimes adds variance in latency

11:15 Priya Reddy: our SLO is 100ms TTFT for typed message case. is that achievable on Dedicated?
11:28 Marcus Li: 100ms is aggressive but doable with streaming + optimized kernels + pre-warmed KV cache and lower sequence lengths. also tuning batch size (to near 1 for interactive) and using smaller context window for initial token helps

13:40 Elena Gomez: question on sequence length -- we're truncating history to 512 for cost reasons. when you say shorter seq length helps TTFT, is that linear?
13:55 Marcus Li: roughly. attention compute scales O(n^2) for full self-attention, so going from 1024 to 512 cuts a chunk out of compute. but in practice the kernel selection and whether kv cache is hot matter too. streaming helps because you can start generating without decoding the entire sequence in some setups

16:10 Samir Khan: our infra: Dedicated pilot uses 2x A100s with shared pool, we're hitting contention during spikes. any quick wins?
16:25 Marcus Li: pre-warm strategies: keep a lightweight reserved slot warm for interactive traffic, or use short-lived warm containers with periodic pings. also configuring priority routing for low-latency tier helps avoid queueing behind batch jobs

18:40 Elena Gomez: about kernel choices, we tried enabling the 'fast-fused' compilation last week and saw 15% throughput improvement but first-token times got worse by ~30ms on small inputs
18:58 Marcus Li: that makes sense. fused paths favor steady-state throughput; for interactive, we recommend using fused for generation at high concurrency but using non-fused or mixed modes for low-latency 1-token response — Redwood runtime supports per-route kernel overrides so you can canary the change

21:30 Ravi Patel: ok what about batching — we love batching for cost but it's killing our latency spikes when a burst arrives
21:45 Marcus Li: continuous batching is workload aware; you can set maximum batching delay (e.g., 10ms) and the runtime will flush for the low-latency tier earlier. another lever is adaptive batching where we target batch size only when queue depth is above a threshold

23:10 Elena Gomez: any tips for measuring TTFT correctly? our instrumentation measures request arrival to end-of-stream, which inflates numbers
23:25 Marcus Li: measure first-byte time at the edge or instrument server-side the earliest write of token 1. for streaming use first-token emitted timestamp. we can share a small script we use to calculate 1-token TTFT from HTTP chunked responses

25:00 Priya Reddy: security question: streaming means partial outputs leave the server sooner — any compliance concerns with PII leaving chunked responses?
25:15 Sofia Chen: good call. from a compliance perspective nothing new — data in transit is still encrypted; you might want to ensure audit logging captures partial outputs if your workflow requires full trace for audit. Redwood supports audit logs and KMS integrations, and we can show how logs tie to chunks if needed

27:40 Marcus Li: demo time — i have a short walkthrough of three config knobs: streaming on/off, kernel mode (fused vs mixed), and batch delay. showed a quick local run: with streaming + mixed kernels + pre-warm we got 1-token TTFT ~50-70ms at 50% concurrency, without streaming we were 140-200ms

31:10 Elena Gomez: thats promising. are those numbers from Hosted or Dedicated?
31:20 Marcus Li: that's from Dedicated pilot on 2xA100 with our mixed-kernel profile; Hosted numbers are similar on comparable hardware but in multi-tenant scenarios variability goes up slightly

33:05 Ravi Patel: action item for us: we'll run a controlled test — enable streaming for a small percentage of traffic, run with mixed kernels, and capture first-token times and p99s

35:30 Samir Khan: for the Dedicated pilot can we pin a tiny reserved pool for interactive traffic? we don't want batch jobs to eat our latency tier
35:45 Sofia Chen: yes, dedicated capacity supports reserved pools and routing policies; we'll include recommended config for a small reserved pool and autoscale thresholds in the doc

38:10 Marcus Li: also note quantization: we saw int8 gave cheaper tokens but sometimes increased jitter. for latency SLOs people pick int8 for throughput-focused endpoints and int16 or fp16 for low-latency endpoints where jitter matters more

40:00 Priya Reddy: can you share the benchmark sheet and which columns to look at?
40:10 Sofia Chen: yep we'll upload the benchmarks spreadsheet to the shared drive — look at '1-token TTFT (streaming)', '1-token TTFT (non-streaming)', 'p50/p95/p99 latency', and kernel flags column. link will be in the follow-up notes

42:30 Elena Gomez: one more question — any quick config to reduce cold-start from 220ms?
42:40 Marcus Li: for cold-starts you can: pre-warm weights in a reserved pool, use lighter-weight container images, keep a tiny standby replica, and tune GC on the host. also use fast model loading paths (quantized checkpoints load faster)

44:00 Sofia Chen: ok recap: Marcus will share kernel selection + sample config, elena will run TTFT with streaming and upload logs, samir to confirm pre-warm strategy, sofia to share pricing impact and upload benchmark sheet. we'll meet next Tuesday same time. thanks all

End of transcript
